Quan Zhou, a multidisciplinary artist born in Cádiz, Spain in 1989 to Chinese parents, has spent years exploring what it means to grow up visibly different in a country that often assumes Spanish identity comes with certain features. Her work—including the graphic novel "Gazpacho agridulce" (Bittersweet Gazpacho) and the podcast "Mi familia española"—examines the experience of being a racialized Spaniard with warmth, data, and a touch of humor. She recalls a childhood moment when her caretaker told her to look in the mirror to see her "slanted eyes," a memory that captures the confusion of discovering you're perceived as different when you've always felt normal.
Zhou's daily reality includes strangers complimenting her Spanish—despite speaking with a perfect Andalusian accent—and locals in her own region addressing her in English, assuming she's a tourist. These moments, absurd and persistent, reflect a broader pattern of never quite being seen as "from here," even when home is the only place you've ever known. Now in her thirties and working within more thoughtful circles, she finds these encounters less painful, though no less frequent. Her creative work investigates how children of migrants constantly negotiate between family culture and the society around them, a balancing act that becomes easier once identity feels secure.
This story matters because it illuminates a quietly universal experience: how belonging is often determined by appearance rather than lived reality. Zhou's approach—frank, curious, and generous—offers a window into Spain's evolving multiculturalism and the everyday work of defining oneself when the world keeps offering its own definitions instead.

item.title: At 91, Claudette Soares makes the present smile with the album 'The world is hard for those who don't know how to wait'
item.description:
At 91 years old, Brazilian singer Claudette Soares has released an album that honors her storied past while embracing something entirely new. For the first time in a seven-decade recording career that began in 1954, the Rio de Janeiro native presents a collection composed entirely of original songs—no covers, just music written specifically for her. The album, titled "O mundo é ruim para quem não sabe esperar" (The world is hard for those who don't know how to wait), arrives as a testament to patience, artistry, and the enduring vitality of bossa nova.
Produced by Thiago Rabello and conceived by Marcus Preto, the record gathers contributions from luminaries of Brazilian music: bossa nova legends Marcos Valle and Roberto Menescal, alongside contemporary talents like Thalma de Freitas, Nando Reis, and Tim Bernardes. The songs range from jazzy foxtrots reminiscent of 1940s ballrooms to classic bossa melodies that evoke sunlit beaches and blue skies. Soares navigates each with a voice described as suave and elegant, whether she's swinging through upbeat sambas or lingering in the melancholy corners of torch songs. The album's deliciously vintage atmosphere feels both nostalgic and fresh, a careful balance that respects the past without being trapped by it.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is the image of an artist in her tenth decade not resting on legacy, but actively shaping new work. Soares sings about making the present smile, about tears that come and go, about life being much bigger than we imagine. It's a reminder that creativity doesn't retire, and that sometimes the most meaningful debuts happen long after the debut album.

item.title: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
item.description:
A 370-acre stretch of land on the outskirts of Cambridge has returned to the National Trust after six decades, marking the beginning of an ambitious nature restoration effort. The site, called Northfield, lies near Anglesey Abbey and represents the first piece of a larger vision to create a connected wildlife corridor stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of the city.
The timing is particularly significant for Cambridgeshire, one of England's most nature-depleted counties. As the region's population grows rapidly, the need for accessible green space has become more pressing. Northfield's landscape sits at the distinctive meeting point of low-lying fenland and chalk ridge, hosting a chalk stream and archaeological traces of human activity dating back millennia, including the Roman period. The National Trust hopes to nurture habitats where vulnerable species like harvest mice, water voles, and turtle doves can recover and thrive.
What makes this story quietly remarkable is its long-term thinking and collaborative spirit. Rather than imposing a fixed plan, the Trust is inviting local residents to help shape what Northfield will become, holding community sessions to gather input before developing detailed proposals in 2027. It's a patient approach to conservation that acknowledges both ecological urgency and the importance of community connection—a reminder that restoring nature and building human relationship with place can happen together, one reclaimed acre at a time.

item.title: Country diary: Why did some trees fall in the storms and others not? It could be spalting | Kate Blincoe
item.description:
In a Norfolk woodland, a seemingly fragile ash tree with a visible split in its trunk continues to stand, even as two recent storms toppled other trees around it. A father and child set up a trail camera to capture the moment it might fall, but the groaning ash defied expectations while healthier-looking neighbors came down instead.
Investigating the fallen trees reveals their hidden vulnerabilities. One toppled ash was completely hollow, colonized by golden scalycap and honey fungus, whose dark bootlace-like tendrils spread underground from root to root. When different fungi compete for the same wood, they create defensive boundaries using darkly pigmented threads, producing intricate patterns called spalting. These ink-dark markings map the territorial battles happening invisibly within the tree, weakening the wood until wind can finally bring it down. What the timber industry considers a flaw—a sign of compromised, rotting wood—craftspeople treasure for its beauty. The unique variations transform ordinary lumber into art, as seen in wooden bowls and furniture.
This quiet observation offers a reminder that appearances can deceive in nature. The loudly suffering tree persists while seemingly stronger ones fall, their inner battles only revealed in their breaking. The story invites readers to look more closely at fallen trees, to see not just storm damage but hidden ecological dramas—and to appreciate how decay itself can create unexpected beauty, even as a concerned family waits with their camera, watching that spalted giant sway on.

item.title: Award-winning photographer lets once-incarcerated teens tell their own story
item.description:
When artist Vernon Ah Kee reached out to photographer Hoda Afshar in 2023, he carried an urgent message: the mass incarceration of Indigenous youth in Far North Queensland was too overwhelming for his community to confront alone. The statistics are stark—Indigenous children aged 10 to 17 represent just 6 percent of the population but are 20 times more likely to be imprisoned. What emerged from that call is "Code Black/Riot," a photography and video project that hands creative control back to the young people whose stories are so often told by others.
Afshar set up a large-format camera in the backyard of Youth Empowered Towards Independence (YETI) in Cairns and waited. For nine days, she returned to the same spot, allowing trust to build gradually. Eventually, formerly incarcerated teenagers began to engage, asking to help, to take pictures, to participate. Using props—fresh flowers, a handmade mask, Joker makeup, an outstretched arm from outside the frame—the young subjects shaped their own portraits while maintaining anonymity. In one image, a young man wraps himself in an Aboriginal flag, only one eye visible. In another, a youth holds a mask of Melpomene, the Greek symbol of tragedy, over his face. A companion video installation reveals harder truths: testimonies of physical assaults by guards, prolonged "night mode" lockdowns, and a 14-year-old who has been incarcerated five times.
This project, now on display at Buxton Contemporary in Melbourne, is a quiet act of resistance. It reminds us that how we frame a story—what we include, what we leave out, who controls the camera—shapes everything. By letting these teenagers direct their own image, Afshar offers something rare: dignity, agency, and a chance to be seen on their own terms.
